question: Mr. Osei is reviewing a writing task completed by his intermediate class. He notices that Carlos has written 'She must to finish the report before Friday,' Wei has written 'Do you must attend the meeting?', and Fatima has written 'She musts arrive early.' Before giving feedback, Mr. Osei wants to diagnose each error precisely so his responses are targeted rather than vague. What should Mr. Osei identify as the specific grammatical problem in each student's sentence, and how should this diagnosis shape the feedback he gives to each learner?
answer: Mr. Osei should apply his knowledge of the three formal properties that all core modal verbs share before saying anything to the students. Carlos's error ('must to finish') violates the rule that a modal is always followed by a bare infinitive — the base form without 'to'. Mr. Osei should tell Carlos that modal verbs never take 'to' before the following verb and elicit the corrected form: 'She must finish the report.' Wei's error ('Do you must attend?') shows that Wei has applied do-support to a modal, treating 'must' like an ordinary verb. Mr. Osei should explain that modals form questions independently, without borrowing 'do', and guide Wei to produce 'Must you attend the meeting?' Fatima's error ('She musts arrive') adds a third-person singular inflection to the modal, which modals never take. Mr. Osei should point out that unlike regular verbs, modals have no '-s' ending regardless of the subject, so the correct form is 'She must arrive early.' In each case, the module's principle is directly relevant: precise identification of an error depends on knowing what kind of error it is. Without diagnosing Carlos's mistake as a bare-infinitive violation, Wei's as a do-support intrusion, and Fatima's as a false inflection, Mr. Osei's feedback would be vague — he could only sense that something sounds wrong. The metalanguage (bare infinitive, do-support, third-person singular inflection) shapes his thinking before each conversation begins, even if he chooses simpler wording when speaking to the students themselves.
anchor: Precise identification of an error depends on knowing what kind of error it is.
